subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: reviewing progress and changing method [Revision]
passage: “Sumit, you know me, Chaitanya, the boy with the big plans. So here's what happened. Three weeks in, I noticed I hadn't learned anything new. I opened my log to see what I'd been doing: video, video, video. I could nod along with anyone, but if you asked me to write a loop I couldn't. That was embarrassing, honestly. So I flipped it. Now I try a small exercise first, like printing a pattern of stars, and I only open a video when I'm truly stuck. The first week I hated it. By week five I had written a number-guessing game with my own hands. It was a small game, but it was mine, and I could explain every line.”

qa.q: What did Chaitanya see when he opened his log?
qa.a: Video, video, video: he had only been watching.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel about the three weeks with nothing new?
qa.a: Embarrassed and disappointed, since he could nod along but could not write a loop himself.

qa.q: What else could Chaitanya do to check his progress, and why?
qa.a: Ask a friend to look at his exercises each week, since outside feedback can catch gaps he cannot see.

qa.q: How does the change look to Sumit?
qa.a: Sumit, hearing this from Chaitanya, sees someone who noticed a lack of progress and changed method, and may feel encouraged to check personal habits too.

grounding: After three weeks without new skills, a student reviews his log, sees he only watched, and switches to exercises first.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: reviewing progress and changing method [Revision]
passage:
I'm Vinita, Francis's neighbour across the corridor. For most of October, whenever I passed his open door, he was on the bed with his laptop, earphones in, some coding video playing, nodding along.
One evening he knocked and asked to borrow my old maths notebook, the one with squared pages. He'd drawn a table on the first page with three columns: “week”, “what I did”, “what I can now do without help”. The last column was nearly empty for all three weeks.
After that, things looked different from the corridor. The earphones were out. A small exercise book lay open beside the laptop, and he'd type, groan, type again. A video came on only now and then, for a few minutes, then went off.
Last Sunday he showed me a program that guessed my birthday month in four questions. I don't know exactly what changed in his head. But something did.

qa.q: What were the three columns in the table Francis drew?
qa.a: Week, what I did, and what I can now do without help.

qa.q: What might Francis have felt when the last column stayed nearly empty?
qa.a: He was likely disappointed and uneasy, since three weeks of watching had left almost nothing he could do on his own.

qa.q: Which approach could Francis have used from the start, and why?
qa.a: Trying a small exercise first and opening a video only when stuck, because it shows gaps right away instead of after three weeks.

qa.q: How does the change look to Vinita from the corridor?
qa.a: To Vinita it looks like a switch from quiet nodding to active struggle, groaning and typing, which ends in a program that actually works.

grounding: A neighbour sees a student find that weeks of videos gave few new skills, then switch to exercises first with videos only when stuck.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: reviewing progress and changing method [Revision]
passage:
Sunday: Divyansh opens his notes file to add a new topic and stops. The last three weeks of entries say “watched loops part 2”, “watched loops part 3”, “watched functions intro”. He tries to write a function that adds two numbers without looking. Nothing comes.
Tuesday: He writes a new rule on a sticky note: exercise first, video only after fifteen minutes stuck. His cousin Simran, who studies computer science, sends a list of twenty tiny exercises. He does two. The second has him stuck; at the ten-minute mark he nearly opens a video, then rereads his own error and fixes it at minute twelve.
Two Saturdays later: Eleven exercises are ticked. When he does open a video, it's for five minutes on the one thing he couldn't crack. He texts Simran a screenshot of a function he wrote himself 🙂

qa.q: What rule does Divyansh write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Exercise first, video only after fifteen minutes stuck.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling on Sunday when nothing came?
qa.a: He likely felt shaken and let down, discovering that weeks of watching had not built the skill he thought it had.

qa.q: What else could Divyansh add to keep the new method working?
qa.a: A weekly look back at the notes file, asking what can now be done alone, so any slide back into only watching is caught early.

qa.q: How might Simran feel receiving the screenshot?
qa.a: Simran is probably pleased, since the exercise list got used and the function shows real progress, not just videos watched.

grounding: Shows a student reviewing weeks of notes, seeing he only watched videos, and switching to exercises first with videos only when stuck.
